title: What If You Jumped Into a Hole Through the Earth? | What If #2
thought_experiment: Labelled thought experiment: a straight, sealed tunnel through the centre, no heat, no rotation; the vacuum run has no air.

hook_candidates.text: You jump into a hole through Earth. Where do you stop?
Watch this clock. You'll reach China before it hits forty.
What if you fell through the whole Earth?
Dropping through the planet takes thirty-eight minutes. Here's why.
You're falling through Earth's core right now. Can you stop?

parts.text: You jump into a hole through Earth.
The other side is thirty-eight minutes away.
With air inside, drag slows each swing
parts.tts: With air inside, drag slows each swing,

parts.text: until you're stuck at the center.
Gravity pulls you faster and faster.
parts.tts: Gravity pulls you, faster, and faster.

parts.text: But at the center, gravity is zero.
You're at top speed, so you shoot through,
slowing until you reach the far side.

sources: Fall time through a straight tunnel via the centre: about 38 minutes (38 min 11 s) with the PREM density model of the real Earth; 42 min 12 s for a uniform-density Earth. Klotz, A. R. (2015), 'The gravity tunnel in a non-uniform Earth', American Journal of Physics 83, 231, doi:10.1119/1.4898780 (arXiv:1308.1342). Summary: phys.org, 2015-03, 'New way to calculate how long it would take to fall through a hole in the Earth'.
Gravity falls to zero at the centre: shell theorem; Klotz 2015 shows the PREM field decreasing roughly linearly through the core to zero at the centre.
Peak speed at the centre (shown as a bar, not spoken): near 8 km/s for a uniform Earth, Klotz 2015.

Without friction the traveller reaches the far surface with zero speed and falls back, oscillating indefinitely: conservation of energy in the same model (Klotz 2015, Sec. II.3 energy relation; standard textbook 'gravity train' result). With air drag the oscillation decays and the traveller comes to rest at the centre (phys.org notes the textbook answer ignores air drag).

Simplifications, labelled on screen: thought experiment, no heat, no Earth rotation (rotation changes the time by seconds, Klotz 2015). Motion drawn with a simple swing; the clock uses the 38-minute PREM figure.
